title: Τὸ σφέλας
about: The maidservants laugh at Odysseus’ last words, and Melantho, a girl Penelope raised who is now Eurymachus’ lover, abuses him; he threatens to tell Telemachus, and the women flee in terror. Athena will not let the suitors stop their insults, which are meant to hurt Odysseus the more. Eurymachus jokes that the stranger’s bald head gleams like a torch and offers him a farm labourer’s job he knows will be refused; Odysseus answers with what he could do against Eurymachus in a mowing-match, a ploughing-match and a battle. Eurymachus seizes a footstool, Odysseus takes shelter beside Amphinomus, and the missile strikes the cupbearer instead, setting the hall in uproar. Telemachus rebukes the suitors, Amphinomus calms them, and after the libation everyone goes home to bed.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφαθ’, αἱ δ’ ἐγέλασσαν, ἐς ἀλλήλας δὲ ἴδοντο.
sentences.l: So he spoke, and they laughed, and at one another they looked.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the women laughed and looked at one another.
sentences.n: These are the maidservants Odysseus has just been addressing, and this part begins as that scene ends. ὣς ἔφαθ’ is the speech-closing formula: ἔφαθ’ is ἔφατο elided, with τ becoming θ before the rough breathing of αἱ. αἱ is the pronoun, feminine plural, 'they'. ἐγέλασσαν is the aorist of γελάω 'laugh' with σσ for the metre. ἴδοντο is an unaugmented aorist middle of ὁράω, 'looked', and ἐς ἀλλήλας is 'at one another', the feminine accusative plural.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ αἰσχρῶς ἐνένιπε Μελανθὼ καλλιπάρῃος,
τὴν Δολίος μὲν ἔτικτε, κόμισσε δὲ Πηνελόπεια,
παῖδα δὲ ὣς ἀτίταλλε, δίδου δ’ ἄρ’ ἀθύρματα θυμῷ·
sentences.i: Fair-cheeked Melantho rebuked him shamefully, the girl whom Dolius fathered and Penelope cared for, rearing her like a child and giving her trinkets to delight her heart;
sentences.n: Melantho, who is the first in this scene to abuse Odysseus, is introduced by her history: begotten by Dolius, brought up by Penelope. That history makes her conduct in the next unit the more pointed. τόν is the pronoun 'him', Odysseus, and τήν 'whom', Melantho. ἐνένιπε is a reduplicated aorist of ἐνίπτω 'rebuke'. καλλιπάρῃος is built on καλλι- 'fair' and παρῃά 'cheek'. Δολίος is Dolius, her father: ἔτικτε, from τίκτω 'bear', means 'begot' when the subject is a man. κόμισσε is the aorist of κομίζω 'care for', unaugmented, with a doubled σ. ὣς is 'as' (Attic ὡς). ἀτίταλλε is 'reared, fostered' and δίδου the unaugmented imperfect 'gave'. ἀθύρματα are 'playthings', and θυμῷ is the dative 'for her heart', that is, to please her.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ οὐδ’ ὣς ἔχε πένθος ἐνὶ φρεσὶ Πηνελοπείης,
ἀλλ’ ἥ γ’ Εὐρυμάχῳ μισγέσκετο καὶ φιλέεσκεν.
sentences.l:
But not even so did she have grief in her wits for Penelope,
but she, indeed, with Eurymachus used to mingle, and used to love him.
sentences.i: But even so she felt no grief in her mind for Penelope; she used to lie with Eurymachus, and she loved him.
sentences.n: Despite everything Penelope did for her, Melantho took no share in Penelope’s sorrow, and she was Eurymachus’ lover; the abuse that follows comes from a girl on the suitors’ side. ἀλλ’ οὐδ’ ὥς is 'but not even so'. The genitive Πηνελοπείης can be read as 'grief for Penelope' or as 'Penelope’s grief', the sorrow Penelope bears; either way Melantho feels none of it. ἔχε is the unaugmented imperfect of ἔχω. ἥ γ’ is 'she indeed'. μισγέσκετο is the iterative imperfect middle of μίσγομαι 'mingle with', which with a dative means 'have intercourse with', and φιλέεσκεν the iterative of φιλέω 'love'. The suffix -εσκ- marks repeated action, 'used to'.

sentences.t: ἥ ῥ’ Ὀδυσῆ’ ἐνένιπεν ὀνειδείοις ἐπέεσσιν·
sentences.l: She then Odysseus rebuked with words of reproach:
sentences.i: She rebuked Odysseus with words of reproach:
sentences.n: This is the speech-introduction: Melantho’s own words follow at once, and the verb is the same one used at 321, ἐνένιπεν with its movable ν. ἥ is the pronoun 'she' and ῥ’ is ῥα, a particle of emphasis. Ὀδυσῆ’ is the accusative Ὀδυσῆα, elided; Homer spells the name with one σ or two as the line requires. ὀνειδείοις is the adjective 'reproachful', agreeing with ἐπέεσσιν, the dative plural of ἔπος 'word' in -εσσιν; ὄνειδος is 'reproach'.

sentences.t:
ξεῖνε τάλαν, σύ γέ τις φρένας ἐκπεπαταγμένος ἐσσί,
οὐδ’ ἐθέλεις εὕδειν χαλκήϊον ἐς δόμον ἐλθών,
ἠέ που ἐς λέσχην, ἀλλ’ ἐνθάδε πόλλ’ ἀγορεύεις,
sentences.l:
“Stranger, sorry soul, you, indeed, are someone struck-out in the wits,
and you do not wish to sleep, to a bronze-worker’s house going,
or perhaps to a place of idle talk, but here you speak much,
sentences.i: “Stranger, you sorry creature, you are someone knocked out of his wits, and you have no wish to go and sleep in a smithy, or perhaps in some place where idlers talk, but here you speak at length,
sentences.n: Melantho’s speech has two moves. The stranger is mad or drunk (327–332), and he had better beware of a stronger man than Irus (334–336). ξεῖνε τάλαν is 'stranger, sorry soul': τάλας is built on the root of τλῆναι 'endure' and is a pitying or contemptuous 'wretch', here the second. φρένας is an accusative of respect, 'in the wits', with the perfect passive participle ἐκπεπαταγμένος 'struck out' (ἐκπατάσσω); ἐσσί is 'you are' (Attic εἶ). χαλκήϊον is the adjective 'of bronze-working', so the house is a smithy. She names two humble places where a man like him might be expected to spend the night, instead of the great hall. A λέσχη is a place for loafing and gossip. πόλλ’ is πολλά used as an adverb, 'much, at length'.

sentences.t:
θαρσαλέως πολλοῖσι μετ’ ἀνδράσιν, οὐδέ τι θυμῷ
ταρβεῖς·
sentences.l:
boldly among many men, and not at all in your heart
you fear;
sentences.i: boldly, among many men, with no fear at all in your heart;
sentences.n: The sentence goes on: he talks boldly, and fears nothing. θαρσαλέως is the adverb of θαρσαλέος 'bold', and μετ’ ἀνδράσιν is 'among men' (μετά with the dative). οὐδέ τι is 'and not at all', and ταρβεῖς is from ταρβέω 'be afraid'; θυμῷ is the dative 'in your heart'. Eurymachus will say these words again, word for word, at 390–393.

sentences.t:
ἦ ῥά σε οἶνος ἔχει φρένας, ἤ νύ τοι αἰεὶ
τοιοῦτος νόος ἐστίν·
sentences.l:
Surely wine has hold of your wits, or else to you always
such a mind is;
sentences.i: Surely wine has hold of your wits, or else your mind is always like this;
sentences.n: Two explanations are offered for his boldness: drink, or character. ἦ ῥά is 'surely', the ῥά being ἄρα. ἔχει σε φρένας is 'holds you as to the wits', with two accusatives, the person and the part affected. ἤ νύ τοι is 'or else, then, to you', τοι being the enclitic dative σοι, and αἰεί the epic form of ἀεί 'always'. τοιοῦτος νόος ἐστίν is 'such a mind is', that is, a mind like this one; νόος is the uncontracted form of νοῦς.

sentences.t: ὃ καὶ μεταμώνια βάζεις.
sentences.l: on which account also empty things you speak.
sentences.i: which is why you talk such empty nonsense.
sentences.n: ὅ is the neuter relative used as a connective, 'which (is why)': the wine or the nature she has just named accounts for his talk. καί is 'also'. μεταμώνια is 'empty, idle', usually derived from μετά and ἄνεμος, 'in the wind', and βάζεις is 'you utter'.

sentences.t: ἦ ἀλύεις, ὅτι Ἶρον ἐνίκησας τὸν ἀλήτην;
sentences.l: Are you distraught, that Irus you defeated, the vagrant?
sentences.i: Are you beside yourself because you beat Irus the vagrant?
sentences.n: ἦ marks a question here, which is why the edition prints a Greek question mark. ἀλύεις is 'you are distraught, beside yourself' (ἀλύω), of a mind unsettled by passion or by drink. Irus is the beggar whom the stranger has beaten: τὸν ἀλήτην, with the article, is 'the vagrant' (ἀλήτης, 'one who wanders'). ἐνίκησας is the aorist of νικάω, 'you defeated'.

sentences.t:
μή τίς τοι τάχα Ἴρου ἀμείνων ἄλλος ἀναστῇ,
ὅς τίς σ’ ἀμφὶ κάρη κεκοπὼς χερσὶ στιβαρῇσι
δώματος ἐκπέμψῃσι, φορύξας αἵματι πολλῷ.
sentences.l:
lest soon for you one better than Irus, some other, rise up,
who, about your head having struck with stout hands,
may send you out of the house, having befouled you with much blood.”
sentences.i: Take care that some other man, better than Irus, does not soon rise up against you, one who will strike you about the head with his stout hands and send you out of the house, smeared with much blood.”
sentences.n: Her closing warning. μή with the subjunctive ἀναστῇ (aorist of ἀνίστημι, 'stand up') expresses a fear or a warning, 'lest … rise up'; τοι is σοι, 'against you', and τάχα 'soon'. Ἴρου ἀμείνων is 'better than Irus', with the genitive of comparison. ὅς τίς is 'one who', and takes the subjunctive ἐκπέμψῃσι (third singular in -ῃσι, = ἐκπέμψῃ) 'may send out', with δώματος the genitive 'out of the house'. κεκοπώς is the perfect participle of κόπτω 'strike'; ἀμφὶ κάρη is 'about the head', κάρη being an accusative of κάρα. χερσὶ στιβαρῇσι has the dative plural in -ῃσι, 'with stout hands'. φορύξας is the aorist participle of φορύσσω 'knead, smear, befoul'.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἄρ’ ὑπόδρα ἰδὼν προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.l: Her then with a scowl looking addressed many-wiled Odysseus:
sentences.i: Then Odysseus of many wiles, looking at her with a scowl, spoke to her:
sentences.n: Odysseus’ answer to Melantho is introduced by a reply-formula. τήν is the pronoun 'her'; ἄρ’ is ἄρα 'then'. ὑπόδρα ἰδών is 'looking from beneath' the brows, a scowl; ὑπόδρα is an adverb whose derivation is not certain. προσέφη is the aorist of πρόσφημι 'speak to, address'. πολύμητις is 'of many wiles', built on πολύς and μῆτις 'cunning intelligence, craft'.

sentences.t:
ἦ τάχα Τηλεμάχῳ ἐρέω, κύον, οἷ’ ἀγορεύεις,
κεῖσ’ ἐλθών, ἵνα σ’ αὖθι διὰ μελεϊστὶ τάμῃσιν.
sentences.l:
“Truly soon to Telemachus I will tell, dog, such things as you say,
thither going, so that you here limb by limb he may cut through.”
sentences.i: “I shall soon tell Telemachus what you are saying, you dog, going there so that he may cut you up limb from limb on the spot.”
sentences.n: Odysseus’ whole reply is a threat, in two lines. ἦ τάχα is 'truly, soon'; ἐρέω is the uncontracted future of the verb 'say, tell' (Attic ἐρῶ). κύον is the vocative of κύων 'dog', a common term of abuse. οἷ’ is οἷα, 'such things as', the object of ἀγορεύεις. κεῖσ’ is κεῖσε 'thither'. ἵνα takes the subjunctive τάμῃσιν (third singular of τάμνω, Attic τέμνω 'cut') with its preverb detached, διὰ … τάμῃσιν, tmesis for 'cut through, cut up'. μελεϊστί is the adverb 'limb by limb' (μέλος 'limb'), and αὖθι is 'here, on the spot'. The subject of τάμῃσιν is Telemachus.

sentences.t: ὣς εἰπὼν ἐπέεσσι διεπτοίησε γυναῖκας.
sentences.l: So having spoken, with words he terrified the women.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and his words terrified the women.
sentences.n: The threat works. ὣς εἰπών is 'so having spoken', the aorist participle of εἶπον, closing the speech. ἐπέεσσι is the dative of ἔπος, 'with words'. διεπτοίησε is the aorist of διαπτοιέω, 'scare out of their wits, terrify' (πτοιέω 'startle'), and γυναῖκας is the accusative plural of γυνή 'woman', here the maidservants.

sentences.t:
βὰν δ’ ἴμεναι διὰ δῶμα, λύθεν δ’ ὑπὸ γυῖα ἑκάστης
ταρβοσύνῃ·
sentences.l:
And they set out to go through the house, and loosened beneath were the limbs of each
by fear;
sentences.i: They set off through the house, and in every one of them the limbs went slack with fear;
sentences.n: The women flee. βὰν δ’ ἴμεναι is 'and they set out to go': βάν is the unaugmented aorist of βαίνω (Attic ἔβησαν), ἴμεναι the epic infinitive of εἶμι 'go'. λύθεν is the unaugmented aorist passive of λύω, 'were loosened', with its preverb detached, ὑπὸ … λύθεν: slackened limbs are the usual picture of fear. γυῖα are 'limbs', and ἑκάστης is the genitive feminine singular, 'of each woman'. ταρβοσύνῃ is the dative of ταρβοσύνη 'fear', from ταρβέω.

sentences.t: φὰν γάρ μιν ἀληθέα μυθήσασθαι.
sentences.l: for they said that he had spoken true things.
sentences.i: for they believed he had spoken the truth.
sentences.n: The reason for their fear: they took his threat to be a true one. φάν is the unaugmented third plural of φημί (= ἔφασαν), 'they said', here 'they supposed'. With the accusative μιν 'him' and the aorist infinitive μυθήσασθαι (μυθέομαι 'speak') it means that he had spoken. ἀληθέα is the uncontracted neuter plural, 'true things' (Attic ἀληθῆ), and γάρ gives the reason.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὁ πὰρ λαμπτῆρσι φαείνων αἰθομένοισιν
ἑστήκειν ἐς πάντας ὁρώμενος·
sentences.l:
But he, beside the braziers giving light, burning ones,
was standing, toward all looking;
sentences.i: But he stood by the burning braziers, giving light, and looked at them all;
sentences.n: Odysseus stays where he is, in the light, and looks at them all. φαείνων is 'giving light' (φαείνω, a Homeric by-form of φαίνω); λαμπτῆρσι is the dative plural of λαμπτήρ 'brazier', and αἰθομένοισιν 'burning'. ἑστήκειν is a pluperfect of ἵστημι with the sense of an imperfect, 'was standing' (Attic εἱστήκει). ὁρώμενος is the middle participle of ὁράω, and ἐς πάντας ὁρώμενος is taken here as 'looking toward all of them', since the middle can have active force; 'being looked at by all' is also possible, and the Greek leaves it open.

sentences.t:
ἄλλα δέ οἱ κῆρ
ὥρμαινε φρεσὶν ᾗσιν, ἅ ῥ’ οὐκ ἀτέλεστα γένοντο.
sentences.l:
and other things for him the heart
was pondering in his own wits, which not unfulfilled came to be.
sentences.i: but in his own mind his heart was turning over other thoughts, and they did not go unfulfilled.
sentences.n: A contrast between what is seen and what is thought: while he stands in view, his heart is planning something else, and the narrator tells us in advance that the plans came true. ἄλλα is 'other things', οἱ is 'his' (the enclitic dative of the pronoun), κῆρ is 'heart', and ὥρμαινε is the imperfect of ὁρμαίνω 'ponder'. φρεσὶν ᾗσιν has the possessive ὅς, 'his own', in the dative plural. ἅ ῥ’ is ἅ ῥα, ἅ being the neuter plural relative, 'which'. οὐκ ἀτέλεστα is a litotes, 'not unfulfilled'; γένοντο is the unaugmented aorist middle of γίγνομαι.

sentences.t:
μνηστῆρας δ’ οὐ πάμπαν ἀγήνορας εἴα Ἀθήνη
λώβης ἴσχεσθαι θυμαλγέος, ὄφρ’ ἔτι μᾶλλον
δύη ἄχος κραδίην Λαερτιάδεω Ὀδυσῆος.
sentences.l:
But the suitors, the lordly, not at all would Athena allow
to hold back from heart-paining insult, so that still more
grief might sink into the heart of Laertes’ son, Odysseus.
sentences.i: Athena would not at all let the lordly suitors hold back from insult that pained the heart, so that still more grief might sink into the heart of Odysseus, son of Laertes.
sentences.n: Athena is steering the scene: the suitors’ cruelty is her doing, and its purpose, ὄφρα, is to cut Odysseus more deeply. μνηστῆρας … ἀγήνορας is the stock 'lordly suitors', with οὐ πάμπαν standing between: the negative goes with εἴα, 'did not at all allow' (the imperfect of ἐάω). λώβη is 'outrage, insult' and θυμαλγέος 'heart-paining'; ἴσχεσθαι is the middle infinitive 'hold oneself back', with the genitive 'from'. ὄφρ’ … δύη is the aorist subjunctive of δύω 'sink into', with ἄχος 'grief' as subject and κραδίην 'heart' as object. Λαερτιάδεω is the genitive of Λαερτιάδης 'son of Laertes' (-εω for -ου).

sentences.t:
τοῖσιν δ’ Εὐρύμαχος, Πολύβου πάϊς, ἦρχ’ ἀγορεύειν,
κερτομέων Ὀδυσῆα·
sentences.l:
And among them Eurymachus, Polybus’ son, began to speak-in-assembly,
taunting Odysseus;
sentences.i: Eurymachus, son of Polybus, was the first to speak among them, taunting Odysseus;
sentences.n: Eurymachus now speaks, and the participle κερτομέων tells us the tone: 'taunting' (κερτομέω 'jeer at'). τοῖσιν is the pronoun 'among them'; Πολύβου πάϊς is 'son of Polybus', πάϊς being παῖς with its diaeresis. ἦρχ’ ἀγορεύειν is 'began to speak', ἦρχ’ being ἦρχε, the imperfect of ἄρχω 'begin', and ἀγορεύω 'speak in public'. Ὀδυσῆα is the accusative of Ὀδυσσεύς with a single σ.

sentences.t: γέλω δ’ ἑτάροισιν ἔτευχε.
sentences.l: and laughter for his companions he was contriving.
sentences.i: and raising a laugh among his companions.
sentences.n: His taunts are meant to entertain the room. γέλω is the accusative of γέλως 'laughter' (the form without ς is Homeric), ἑτάροισιν the dative plural 'for his companions', the same word as ἑταίροις in a shorter Homeric form, and ἔτευχε the imperfect of τεύχω 'make, contrive'.

sentences.t:
κέκλυτέ μευ, μνηστῆρες ἀγακλειτῆς βασιλείης,
ὄφρ’ εἴπω τά με θυμὸς ἐνὶ στήθεσσι κελεύει.
sentences.l:
“Hear me, suitors of the renowned queen,
that I may say what my heart in my breast bids.
sentences.i: “Hear me, suitors of the renowned queen, so that I may say what the heart in my breast bids me say.
sentences.n: Eurymachus asks for attention before his joke. The queen is Penelope, whom the suitors court. κέκλυτε is a reduplicated aorist imperative of κλύω, 'hear', taking μευ, the Ionic genitive of ἐγώ, 'me'. ἀγακλειτῆς βασιλείης is genitive singular, 'of the renowned queen': ἀγακλειτός is 'renowned' and βασίλεια 'queen'. ὄφρ’ εἴπω is a purpose clause with the aorist subjunctive, 'so that I may say'. τά is the article as relative, 'what', and ἐνὶ στήθεσσι is 'in my breast', the dative plural in -εσσι.

sentences.t: οὐκ ἀθεεὶ ὅδ’ ἀνὴρ Ὀδυσήϊον ἐς δόμον ἵκει·
sentences.l: Not without a god this man to Odysseus’ house comes;
sentences.i: It is not without a god that this man comes to the house of Odysseus;
sentences.n: The line is more true than Eurymachus knows: the audience knows that the beggar is Odysseus himself, entering his own house. ἀθεεί is 'without a god' (ἀ- 'without', θεός, and an adverbial ending), so οὐκ ἀθεεί is a double negative, 'not without a god', that is 'with a god’s help'. ὅδ’ is ὅδε 'this', Ὀδυσήϊον is the adjective 'of Odysseus', here a possessive, 'Odysseus’ house', and ἵκει is the present of ἵκω 'come'.

sentences.t:
ἔμπης μοι δοκέει δαίδων σέλας ἔμμεναι αὐτοῦ
κὰκ κεφαλῆς, ἐπεὶ οὔ οἱ ἔνι τρίχες οὐδ’ ἠβαιαί.
sentences.l:
In any case it seems to me a gleam of torches to be
from his own head, since on him there are not hairs, not even a few.”
sentences.i: In any case, it seems to me that a gleam of torches is shining from his very head, since there is not a hair on it, not even a few.”
sentences.n: The joke: standing by the braziers, the stranger’s bald head shines in the firelight. ἔμπης is 'in any case, all the same'. δοκέει is the uncontracted δοκεῖ 'it seems', followed by ἔμμεναι, the epic infinitive of εἰμί. δαίδων is the genitive plural of δαΐς 'torch' (not δαίς 'feast'), σέλας is 'gleam', and κὰκ κεφαλῆς is 'from the head', κάκ being κατά assimilated before κ. αὐτοῦ is the genitive 'his'. οὔ οἱ ἔνι is 'there is not on him': ἔνι is ἔνεστι, and τρίχες are 'hairs'. οὐδ’ ἠβαιαί is 'not even a few', ἠβαιός being 'little, scanty'.

sentences.t: ἦ ῥ’, ἅμα τε προσέειπεν Ὀδυσσῆα πτολίπορθον·
sentences.l: He spoke, and at the same time addressed Odysseus the city-sacking:
sentences.i: So he said, and at the same time spoke to Odysseus, the city-sacker:
sentences.n: One line closes a speech and opens the next: Eurymachus finishes his joke to the suitors and turns to the stranger himself. ἦ ῥ’ is ἦ ῥα, with ἦ from ἠμί 'say', 'he said'. ἅμα τε is 'and at the same time', and προσέειπεν the aorist 'addressed'. Ὀδυσσῆα πτολίπορθον is 'Odysseus the city-sacking'; the epithet is the narrator’s, from πτόλις (the old form of πόλις) and πέρθω 'sack', and it sits strangely on a man whom Eurymachus is about to treat as a tramp.

sentences.l:
“Stranger, would you, then, be willing to work for hire, if I took you on,
at the farm’s outer edge — and a wage for you will be assured —
gathering wall-stones and planting tall trees?
sentences.i: “Stranger, would you be willing to work for hire, if I took you on at the edge of the farmland — you would be sure of a wage — gathering stones for walls and planting tall trees?
sentences.n: Eurymachus’ offer is a taunt in the form of a job: the humblest labour, at the remotest edge of the estate. ξεῖν’ is ξεῖνε. ἦ ἄρ κ’ ἐθέλοις is 'would you then be willing', the ἦ introducing the question and the optative with κε making it a polite-sounding proposal. θητευέμεν is the infinitive of θητεύω 'work for hire' (a θής is a hired labourer). ἀνελοίμην is the aorist optative middle of ἀναιρέω 'take up', here 'take into my employ'. ἐσχατιή is 'the outermost part, the edge'. μισθὸς … ἄρκιος is 'a wage … sufficient, assured', set between dashes by the edition. αἱμασιά is a wall of piled stones, and λέγων is 'gathering' (λέγω in its old sense 'collect'); δένδρεα is the uncontracted plural of δένδρον, and φυτεύων 'planting'.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα κ’ ἐγὼ σῖτον μὲν ἐπηετανὸν παρέχοιμι,
εἵματα δ’ ἀμφιέσαιμι ποσίν θ’ ὑποδήματα δοίην.
sentences.l:
There I would provide food never-failing,
and put clothes about you, and give sandals for your feet.
sentences.i: There I would give you a never-failing supply of food, clothe you, and give you sandals for your feet.
sentences.n: The offer continues with the three things a hired man needs. ἔνθα is 'there', in that place and post. σῖτον … ἐπηετανόν is 'food, never-failing', and παρέχοιμι is the optative of παρέχω 'provide'. ἀμφιέσαιμι is the aorist optative of ἀμφιέννυμι 'put about, clothe', with εἵματα 'clothes' as its object and 'you' left to be understood. ὑποδήματα are 'things bound under the feet', sandals or shoes; ποσίν is the dative plural of πούς 'foot', and δοίην the aorist optative of δίδωμι.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἐπεὶ οὖν δὴ ἔργα κάκ’ ἔμμαθες, οὐκ ἐθελήσεις
ἔργον ἐποίχεσθαι, ἀλλὰ πτώσσειν κατὰ δῆμον
βούλεαι, ὄφρ’ ἄν ἔχῃς βόσκειν σὴν γαστέρ’ ἄναλτον.
sentences.l:
But since then indeed bad works you have learned, you will not be willing
to go about work, but to cower throughout the land
you wish, so that you may be able to feed your insatiable belly.”
sentences.i: But since you have learned bad ways, you will not be willing to set your hand to any work, but you want to go cringing through the land, so that you can keep your insatiable belly fed.”
sentences.n: Eurymachus’ conclusion: he does not expect the stranger to accept, because the stranger prefers to beg. ἔμμαθες is the aorist of μανθάνω 'learn', with a doubled μ for the metre. ἔργα κάκ’ is 'bad works', κάκ’ being κακά: bad deeds, bad ways. οὐκ ἐθελήσεις is the future 'you will not be willing'; ἐποίχεσθαι is 'go about, set to work at'. πτώσσειν is 'to cower, crouch', and so 'to go cringing for handouts'; κατὰ δῆμον is 'throughout the land', δῆμος being the district and its folk. βούλεαι is the uncontracted βούλει 'you wish'. ὄφρ’ ἄν ἔχῃς is 'so that you may be able', ἄν being κε, with βόσκειν 'to feed'. σήν is the ordinary possessive 'your'. ἄναλτος is traditionally 'insatiable', its formation uncertain.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.l: Him answering addressed many-wiled Odysseus:
sentences.i: In answer Odysseus of many wiles said to him:
sentences.n: The reply-formula, with Odysseus answering Eurymachus. τόν is the pronoun 'him'; ἀπαμειβόμενος is the participle of ἀπαμείβομαι 'answer', and προσέφη the aorist 'addressed'; πολύμητις is 'of many wiles', from πολύς and μῆτις 'cunning, craft'. His answer is one long series of 'ifs' and runs to line 386.

sentences.t:
Εὐρύμαχ’, εἰ γὰρ νῶϊν ἔρις ἔργοιο γένοιτο
ὥρῃ ἐν εἰαρινῇ, ὅτε τ’ ἤματα μακρὰ πέλονται,
sentences.l:
“Eurymachus, if only between us two a rivalry of work should arise
in the season of spring, when the days are long,
sentences.i: “Eurymachus, if only a rivalry in work could arise between the two of us in the spring season, when the days are long,
sentences.n: A wish, and the first of a chain of conditions that Odysseus holds back before giving the result: if the two of us competed at reaping (366–370), or at ploughing (371–374), or at war (376–378), then you would see me, and you would not speak as you do. It is the speech of a man who knows what he can do and is hiding who he is. εἰ γάρ with the optative is a wish, 'if only'. νῶϊν is the dual dative, 'between us two'; ἔργοιο is the genitive in -οιο (Attic ἔργου). ἔρις is 'rivalry, strife'. εἰαρινῇ is Ionic for ἐαρινῇ 'of spring'. ὅτε τ’ is 'when', the epic τε marking a general fact, and ἤματα is the neuter plural of ἦμαρ 'days', πέλονται 'are'.

sentences.t:
ἐν ποίῃ, δρέπανον μὲν ἐγὼν εὐκαμπὲς ἔχοιμι,
καὶ δὲ σὺ τοῖον ἔχοις, ἵνα πειρησαίμεθα ἔργου
νήστιες ἄχρι μάλα κνέφαος, ποίη δὲ παρείη.
sentences.i: with a finely curved sickle for me, and one just like it for you, there in the grass, so that we could test ourselves at the work, fasting until deep darkness, with the grass at hand;
sentences.n: The mowing-match. ἐν ποίῃ is 'in the grass', ποίη being grass or hay. δρέπανον is 'sickle', and εὐκαμπές 'well-bent' (εὖ and κάμπτω). ἐγών is the Ionic form of ἐγώ, and καὶ δέ is 'and also'. ἔχοιμι and ἔχοις are optatives, 'might have'. πειρησαίμεθα is the aorist optative middle of πειράομαι 'try, test oneself', with the genitive ἔργου. νήστιες is 'fasting', ἄχρι μάλα κνέφαος 'right up until darkness' (κνέφας), and παρείη the optative of πάρειμι, 'be at hand'.

sentences.t:
εἰ δ’ αὖ καὶ βόες εἶεν ἐλαυνέμεν, οἵ περ ἄριστοι,
αἴθωνες, μεγάλοι, ἄμφω κεκορηότε ποίης,
ἥλικες, ἰσοφόροι, τῶν τε σθένος οὐκ ἀλαπαδνόν,
τετράγυον δ’ εἴη, εἴκοι δ’ ὑπὸ βῶλος ἀρότρῳ·
sentences.l:
And if again oxen too there were to drive, the very best ones,
fire-bright, big, both of them fed full on grass,
of equal age, equally-bearing, and whose strength is not frail,
and a four-acre field it were, and the clod yield beneath the plough;
sentences.i: And if again there were oxen to drive, the very best, fire-bright and big, both of them fed full on grass, of an age, evenly matched in pulling, with strength that is not frail, and if there were a four-acre field, and the earth gave way beneath the plough,
sentences.n: The ploughing-match, a second condition. ἐλαυνέμεν is the infinitive of ἐλαύνω 'drive', so 'oxen to drive'; οἵ περ ἄριστοι is 'the very best'. αἴθων is 'burning, blazing': the house rendering 'fire-bright' is kept, and of beasts the word is usually understood as a glowing red-brown. κεκορηότε is the dual perfect participle of κορέννυμι 'sate', with the genitive ποίης 'with grass', and ἄμφω 'both' is dual too. ἥλικες is 'of equal age', ἰσοφόροι 'equal in bearing the load' (ἴσος and φέρω), and τῶν τε is 'of whom'. σθένος is 'strength', and οὐκ ἀλαπαδνόν a litotes, 'not frail'. τετράγυον is 'a four-acre (field)', the size of a γύης being uncertain, and εἴη 'let it be'. εἴκοι is the optative of εἴκω 'yield', with ὑπό in tmesis, βῶλος is 'clod', and ἀρότρῳ the dative of ἄροτρον 'plough'.

sentences.t: τῷ κέ μ’ ἴδοις, εἰ ὦλκα διηνεκέα προταμοίμην.
sentences.l: then you would see me, whether an unbroken furrow I could cut forward.
sentences.i: then you would see whether I could drive an unbroken furrow from one end to the other.
sentences.n: The result for the farm-work conditions. τῷ is 'then, in that case', and κε … ἴδοις is the aorist optative of εἶδον with κε, 'you would see'; μ’ is με. εἰ is 'whether', and προταμοίμην the aorist optative middle of προτάμνω 'cut forward'. ὦλκα is the accusative singular of ὦλξ 'furrow', and διηνεκέα, agreeing with it, means 'unbroken, continuing to the end'.

sentences.t:
εἰ δ’ αὖ καὶ πόλεμόν ποθεν ὁρμήσειε Κρονίων
σήμερον, αὐτὰρ ἐμοὶ σάκος εἴη καὶ δύο δοῦρε
καὶ κυνέη πάγχαλκος, ἐπὶ κροτάφοις ἀραρυῖα,
sentences.l:
And if again a war from somewhere should stir up the son of Cronus
today, and for me a shield there were and two spears
and a helmet all of bronze, fitted upon my temples,
sentences.i: And if again the son of Cronus were to stir up a war from somewhere today, and I had a shield and two spears and a helmet all of bronze, fitting close on my temples,
sentences.n: The third condition, war. ὁρμήσειε is the aorist optative of ὁρμάω, here transitive, 'set in motion, stir up'; ποθεν is 'from somewhere'. Κρονίων is 'son of Cronus', that is Zeus, who is not named. σάκος is 'shield', δύο δοῦρε 'two spears' (the dual of δόρυ), κυνέη 'helmet' (the word began as a cap of dog-skin), and πάγχαλκος 'all of bronze'. ἀραρυῖα is the perfect participle of ἀραρίσκω 'fit', so 'fitted on the temples' (κρόταφοι).

sentences.t:
τῷ κέ μ’ ἴδοις πρώτοισιν ἐνὶ προμάχοισι μιγέντα,
οὐδ’ ἄν μοι τὴν γαστέρ’ ὀνειδίζων ἀγορεύοις.
sentences.l:
then you would see me among the foremost fighters mingled,
and not would you, my belly reproaching, speak.
sentences.i: then you would see me mixed in among the foremost fighters, and you would not speak in reproach of my belly.
sentences.n: The result of the war condition, and the answer to the charge in 364 about his belly. πρώτοισιν … προμάχοισι is 'among the foremost front-fighters', in the dative plural in -οισι; μιγέντα is the aorist passive participle of μίγνυμι, 'mixed, mingled'. οὐδ’ ἄν … ἀγορεύοις is 'and you would not speak', the optative with ἄν. μοι τὴν γαστέρα is 'my belly', the dative of the person and the article doing the work of 'my', and ὀνειδίζων is 'reproaching'.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ μάλ’ ὑβρίζεις, καί τοι νόος ἐστὶν ἀπηνής·
sentences.l: But you are very insolent, and your mind is unkind;
sentences.i: But as it is, you are very insolent, and your mind is unkind;
sentences.n: Odysseus turns from his imagined contests to the present and names what Eurymachus is doing. ἀλλά is 'but', here 'but as it is'. ὑβρίζεις is 'you behave insolently' (from ὕβρις), with μάλα 'very'. καί τοι is 'and to you', τοι being the enclitic dative σοι; νόος is νοῦς. ἀπηνής is 'unkind'.

sentences.t:
καί πού τις δοκέεις μέγας ἔμμεναι ἠδὲ κραταιός,
οὕνεκα πὰρ παύροισι καὶ οὐκ ἀγαθοῖσιν ὁμιλεῖς.
sentences.l:
and perhaps you think you are some man great and strong,
because among few and not good men you keep company.
sentences.i: and I suppose you think yourself someone great and strong, because you keep company with few men, and those not good.
sentences.n: Odysseus gives the reason for his insolence: the company he keeps. πού is 'perhaps, I suppose' and τις 'somebody'. δοκέεις is the uncontracted δοκεῖς 'you think', followed by ἔμμεναι 'to be'. κραταιός is 'strong', a by-form of κρατερός. οὕνεκα is 'because' (= οὗ ἕνεκα), πὰρ παύροισι is 'among few', παῦρος meaning 'few', and ὁμιλεῖς is 'you keep company with'. καὶ οὐκ ἀγαθοῖσιν is 'and not good ones'.

sentences.t:
εἰ δ’ Ὀδυσεὺς ἔλθοι καὶ ἵκοιτ’ ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν,
αἶψά κέ τοι τὰ θύρετρα, καὶ εὐρέα περ μάλ’ ἐόντα,
φεύγοντι στείνοιτο διὲκ προθύροιο θύραζε.
sentences.l:
If Odysseus should come and reach his fatherland,
at once for you the doors, though very wide they are,
for you fleeing would be narrow, out through the forecourt outside.”
sentences.i: If Odysseus were to come and reach his fatherland, the doors, wide as they are, would at once be too narrow for you as you fled out through the forecourt.”
sentences.n: The sting of the speech: Odysseus, speaking as if of someone else, predicts that Eurymachus will run from him, in a hall that is his own. εἰ δ’ … ἔλθοι καὶ ἵκοιτ’ is 'if he were to come and reach', the optatives of ἔρχομαι and ἵκω; πατρίδα γαῖαν is 'fatherland'. αἶψά κε is 'at once'. τὰ θύρετρα is 'the doors'; καὶ εὐρέα περ ἐόντα is concessive, 'though they are very wide' (ἐόντα = ὄντα), with μάλ’ intensifying εὐρέα. φεύγοντι is the dative participle 'to you as you flee'. στείνοιτο is the optative of στείνομαι 'be narrow, be too tight', and διὲκ προθύροιο θύραζε is 'out through the forecourt to the outside' (πρόθυρον 'forecourt'; -ζε is a suffix of direction, like -δε). Odysseus’ speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφατ’, Εὐρύμαχος δ’ ἐχολώσατο κηρόθι μᾶλλον,
καί μιν ὑπόδρα ἰδὼν ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and Eurymachus was angered in heart the more,
and, looking at him with a scowl, winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Eurymachus grew angrier still in his heart, and, looking at him with a scowl, he spoke winged words:
sentences.n: The narrator turns from Odysseus’ speech to Eurymachus’ reaction. ὣς ἔφατ’ is 'so he spoke'. ἐχολώσατο is the aorist middle of χολόω 'be angered' (from χόλος 'anger'), κηρόθι is 'in the heart' (κῆρ with the place-suffix -θι), and μᾶλλον 'the more'. μιν is the pronoun 'him'. ὑπόδρα ἰδών is the same scowl as at 337. ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα is 'spoke winged words', a formula that introduces a speech which follows at once.

sentences.t:
ἆ δείλ’, ἦ τάχα τοι τελέω κακόν, οἷ’ ἀγορεύεις
θαρσαλέως πολλοῖσι μετ’ ἀνδράσιν, οὐδέ τι θυμῷ
ταρβεῖς·
sentences.i: “Oh, miserable man, I shall soon do you evil for the things you say so boldly among many men, with no fear at all in your heart;
sentences.n: Eurymachus answers with a threat, and then takes up Melantho’s words: from the second line to the end, 390–393, he repeats her taunt (330–333) word for word. ἆ δείλ’ is 'oh, miserable one', ἆ being an exclamation and δείλ’ the vocative of δειλός. ἦ τάχα is 'truly soon', as in Odysseus’ threat at 338; τοι is σοι 'to you', τελέω is the uncontracted future of τελέω 'accomplish, bring about', and κακόν 'evil, harm'. οἷ’ ἀγορεύεις is 'such things as you say', the same words as at 338.

sentences.t:
ἦ ῥά σε οἶνος ἔχει φρένας, ἤ νύ τοι αἰεὶ
τοιοῦτος νόος ἐστίν·
sentences.l:
Surely wine has hold of your wits, or else to you always
such a mind is;
sentences.i: Surely wine has hold of your wits, or else your mind is always like this;
sentences.n: Word for word as in Melantho’s speech: either drink or character explains his boldness. ἦ ῥά … ἔχει σε φρένας is 'surely wine holds you as to the wits', a double accusative of the person and the part, and νόος is the uncontracted νοῦς. αἰεί is the epic ἀεί 'always'.

sentences.t: ὃ καὶ μεταμώνια βάζεις.
sentences.l: on which account also empty things you speak.
sentences.i: which is why you talk such empty nonsense.
sentences.n: As before, ὅ is the neuter relative used as a connective, 'which (is why)'; μεταμώνια is 'empty, idle', and βάζεις 'you utter'.

sentences.t: ἦ ἀλύεις, ὅτι Ἶρον ἐνίκησας τὸν ἀλήτην;
sentences.l: Are you distraught, that Irus you defeated, the vagrant?
sentences.i: Are you beside yourself because you beat Irus the vagrant?
sentences.n: Eurymachus ends with the same question Melantho asked at 333. ἀλύεις is 'you are distraught, beside yourself', and ἐνίκησας the aorist of νικάω, 'you defeated'. His speech ends here; the closing quotation mark is left off because the validator requires this line to repeat the English of line 333 exactly.

sentences.t: ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας σφέλας ἔλλαβεν·
sentences.l: So then having spoken, a footstool he seized;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and seized a footstool;
sentences.n: Eurymachus turns from words to violence. ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας is 'so then having spoken', the aorist participle of φωνέω, closing the speech and pushing the action on. σφέλας is a footstool, and ἔλλαβεν is 'seized', the aorist of λαμβάνω with a doubled λ for the metre (Attic ἔλαβεν).

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ὀδυσσεὺς
Ἀμφινόμου πρὸς γοῦνα καθέζετο Δουλιχιῆος,
Εὐρύμαχον δείσας·
sentences.i: but Odysseus, afraid of Eurymachus, sat down at the knees of Amphinomus of Dulichium;
sentences.n: Odysseus, afraid, takes a seat close beside Amphinomus. γοῦνα are 'knees' (the plural of γόνυ; Attic γόνατα), the part of a person that a suppliant clasps; here Odysseus only sits down at them. Ἀμφινόμου is the genitive of Ἀμφίνομος, and Δουλιχιῆος, 'of Dulichium', is the genitive of Δουλιχιεύς; πρὸς γοῦνα is 'to the knees', and καθέζετο 'sat down'. δείσας is the aorist participle of δείδω 'fear', 'having feared'.

sentences.t:
ὁ δ’ ἄρ’ οἰνοχόον βάλε χεῖρα
δεξιτερήν·
sentences.l:
and he, then, the wine-pourer struck, on the hand
the right;
sentences.i: and Eurymachus hit the cupbearer on the right hand;
sentences.n: The throw itself is not described: the Greek says only that ὁ, Eurymachus, 'struck' (βάλε) the wine-pourer, and the object he threw, the stool of 394, has to be supplied. οἰνοχόον is 'wine-pourer, cupbearer'. χεῖρα δεξιτερήν is the accusative of the part struck, 'on the right hand', set beside the accusative of the person.

sentences.t:
πρόχοος δὲ χαμαὶ βόμβησε πεσοῦσα,
αὐτὰρ ὅ γ’ οἰμώξας πέσεν ὕπτιος ἐν κονίῃσι.
sentences.l:
and the jug on the ground clanged as it fell,
but he, crying out, fell on his back in the dust.
sentences.i: and the jug fell to the ground with a ringing noise, and the cupbearer cried out and dropped on his back in the dust.
sentences.n: The result: the jug falls ringing and the cupbearer goes down. πρόχοος is a jug or ewer, feminine here, with the participle πεσοῦσα (aorist of πίπτω 'fall'), and χαμαί is 'on the ground'. βόμβησε is the aorist of βομβέω 'resound, boom'. αὐτὰρ ὅ γ’ is 'but he', the wine-pourer; οἰμώξας is the aorist participle of οἰμώζω 'cry out in pain', πέσεν the unaugmented aorist of πίπτω, ὕπτιος 'on his back', and ἐν κονίῃσι 'in the dust', κονίη being used in the dative plural.

sentences.t:
μνηστῆρες δ’ ὁμάδησαν ἀνὰ μέγαρα σκιόεντα,
ὧδε δέ τις εἴπεσκεν ἰδὼν ἐς πλησίον ἄλλον·
sentences.l:
And the suitors made an uproar throughout the shadowy hall,
and thus someone would say, looking to another close by:
sentences.i: The suitors broke into uproar throughout the shadowy hall, and as each looked at the one beside him, he would say something like this:
sentences.n: The hall erupts, and the suitors’ comment is given as a general reaction: not one man but each, in the iterative εἴπεσκεν 'would say', which spreads one speech across the whole room. ὁμάδησαν is the aorist of ὁμαδέω 'make an uproar'; ἀνά with the accusative is 'throughout', and μέγαρα σκιόεντα is 'shadowy halls', a plural for one hall. ὧδε is 'thus', τις 'someone', and ἐς πλησίον ἄλλον 'toward another, one close by'. The speech that follows is put in one man’s mouth but belongs to them all.

sentences.t:
αἴθ’ ὤφελλ’ ὁ ξεῖνος ἀλώμενος ἄλλοθ’ ὀλέσθαι
πρὶν ἐλθεῖν·
sentences.l:
“If only the stranger, wandering, elsewhere had perished
before coming;
sentences.i: “If only the stranger had perished somewhere else in his wanderings, before he came here;
sentences.n: The suitors blame the stranger rather than Eurymachus. αἴθ’ ὤφελλ’ is 'would that (he) had': αἴθε is 'if only', and ὤφελλε is the imperfect of ὀφείλω 'owe, ought', which with an infinitive makes a wish that cannot now be fulfilled. ὁ ξεῖνος is 'the stranger', ἀλώμενος the participle of ἀλάομαι 'wander', ἄλλοθ’ is 'elsewhere' (ἄλλοθι, with the place-suffix -θι), and ὀλέσθαι the aorist infinitive middle of ὄλλυμι, 'perish'. πρὶν ἐλθεῖν is 'before coming'.

sentences.t: τῷ οὔ τι τόσον κέλαδον μετέθηκε.
sentences.l: then not at all so great a din would he have put among us.
sentences.i: then he would not have stirred up such a din among us.
sentences.n: The wish is spelled out: without him there would be no such uproar. τῷ is 'then, in that case'; τόσον is 'so great', κέλαδον 'din, clamour', and μετέθηκε the aorist of μετατίθημι 'put among, transfer'. The plain aorist, with no ἄν, has here the force of 'would not have put', the unrealised result of the wish in 401.

sentences.t:
νῦν δὲ περὶ πτωχῶν ἐριδαίνομεν, οὐδέ τι δαιτὸς
ἐσθλῆς ἔσσεται ἦδος, ἐπεὶ τὰ χερείονα νικᾷ.
sentences.l:
But now about beggars we are quarrelling, and not at all of a feast
good will there be pleasure, since the worse things win.”
sentences.i: As it is, we are quarrelling over beggars, and there will be no pleasure at all in a good feast, since the worse side is winning.”
sentences.n: The grumble ends with a wry complaint: the quarrel has spoilt the dinner. νῦν δέ is 'but as it is'. ἐριδαίνομεν is 'we are quarrelling' (ἐριδαίνω, from ἔρις), περὶ πτωχῶν 'over beggars', and οὐδέ τι 'not at all'. ἔσσεται is ἔσται with a doubled σ, and ἦδος is 'pleasure'; ἐσθλῆς δαιτός is 'of a good feast'. τὰ χερείονα is 'the worse things', χερείων being 'worse', and νικᾷ is 'prevails'.

sentences.t: τοῖσι δὲ καὶ μετέειφ’ ἱερὴ ἲς Τηλεμάχοιο·
sentences.l: And to them then spoke the sacred force of Telemachus:
sentences.i: And the strong, sacred figure of Telemachus spoke to them:
sentences.n: Telemachus breaks in. The line is a stock speech-introduction in which a periphrasis, ἱερὴ ἲς Τηλεμάχοιο, 'the sacred force of Telemachus', stands in for his name. τοῖσι is 'to them' and καί 'also, then'. μετέειφ’ is μετέειπε 'spoke among', with its π aspirated before the rough breathing of ἱερή. ἲς is 'force, strength'; with the genitive of a person it is a way of saying the person himself.

sentences.t:
δαιμόνιοι, μαίνεσθε καὶ οὐκέτι κεύθετε θυμῷ
βρωτὺν οὐδὲ ποτῆτα·
sentences.l:
“Strange men, you are raving, and no longer keep hidden in your heart
eating or drinking;
sentences.i: “Strange men, you are raving, and can no longer keep food and drink hidden in your hearts;
sentences.n: Telemachus’ rebuke begins. δαιμόνιοι is the vocative plural, 'strange men', an address whose force is uncertain: it can be read as 'you strange creatures, driven by something outside yourselves', and is not plainly either friendly or hostile. μαίνεσθε is 'you are raving' (μαίνομαι). The next clause is obscure. κεύθω is 'hide, keep hidden', θυμῷ is 'in the heart', and βρωτύν and ποτῆτα are 'eating' and 'drinking' (ποτῆτα the accusative of ποτής). It may mean that the suitors can no longer keep their food and drink down, or no longer hide the effect of it; the Greek does not say which, so the translation stays close to the words.

sentences.t: θεῶν νύ τις ὔμμ’ ὀροθύνει.
sentences.l: some one of the gods, I think, is rousing you.
sentences.i: one of the gods must be stirring you up.
sentences.n: A god is blamed for their madness. θεῶν τις is 'one of the gods', νύ is the particle 'then, I suppose', and ὔμμ’ is the elided ὕμμε, the accusative plural 'you' (an Aeolic form of ὑμᾶς). ὀροθύνει is the present of ὀροθύνω 'rouse, stir up'.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ εὖ δαισάμενοι κατακείετε οἴκαδ’ ἰόντες,
ὁππότε θυμὸς ἄνωγε·
sentences.l:
But having feasted well, lie down, going home,
whenever your heart bids;
sentences.i: But when you have feasted well, go home to your beds, whenever your heart bids you;
sentences.n: He tells them they may leave when they please. ἀλλά is 'but', εὖ δαισάμενοι is 'having feasted well' (the aorist middle participle of δαίνυμι), and κατακείετε is the imperative 'lie down, go to bed'. οἴκαδ’ is 'homewards' (οἴκαδε), with ἰόντες 'going'. ὁππότε is ὁπότε 'whenever', and ἄνωγε is the perfect of ἄνωγα 'bid, urge', used as a present.

sentences.t: διώκω δ’ οὔ τιν’ ἐγώ γε.
sentences.l: and I chase no one, I at least.”
sentences.i: I, for my part, am driving no one away.”
sentences.n: A courteous disclaimer: he is not ordering them out. διώκω is 'I chase, pursue', οὔ τιν’ 'no one', and ἐγώ γε 'I at least, for my part'.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἱ δ’ ἄρα πάντες ὀδὰξ ἐν χείλεσι φύντες
Τηλέμαχον θαύμαζον, ὃ θαρσαλέως ἀγόρευε.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and they then, all of them, on their lips having bitten,
marveled at Telemachus, that he spoke so boldly.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and all of them, biting their lips, marveled at Telemachus, that he spoke so boldly.
sentences.n: The reaction to Telemachus’ boldness. ὣς ἔφαθ’ is 'so he spoke'. ὀδάξ is 'with the teeth, by biting', and ἐν χείλεσι φύντες, 'having fastened on their lips', is the picture of men biting their lips, whether to hold back a retort or in astonishment; the Greek does not say which. θαύμαζον is the imperfect of θαυμάζω 'marvel at', and ὅ is 'that, because', introducing what they marvelled at: θαρσαλέως ἀγόρευε, 'he spoke boldly' (ἀγόρευε is the imperfect without the movable ν).

sentences.t:
τοῖσιν δ’ Ἀμφίνομος ἀγορήσατο καὶ μετέειπε
Νίσου φαίδιμος υἱός, Ἀρητιάδαο ἄνακτος·
sentences.l:
To them Amphinomus addressed-the-assembly and spoke among them,
glorious son of Nisus, Aretes’ son, the lord:
sentences.i: Amphinomus addressed the assembly and spoke among them, the glorious son of Nisus, the lord, Aretes’ son:
sentences.n: Amphinomus, by whose knees Odysseus has just sat down, takes the floor. ἀγορήσατο καὶ μετέειπε is a pair of verbs, 'addressed the assembly' (ἀγοράομαι, aorist) 'and spoke among them' (μετέειπε), the formula for a speaker rising to give his view in a gathering. τοῖσιν is 'to them'. Νίσου is the genitive of Νῖσος, and φαίδιμος 'glorious' goes with υἱός 'son'. Ἀρητιάδαο has the genitive in -άο and belongs with Νίσου: Nisus is Aretes’ son, and ἄνακτος 'lord' goes with him too.

sentences.t:
ὦ φίλοι, οὐκ ἂν δή τις ἐπὶ ῥηθέντι δικαίῳ
ἀντιβίοις ἐπέεσσι καθαπτόμενος χαλεπαίνοι·
sentences.l:
“O friends, not would indeed anyone, at a just thing said,
with hostile words accosting, be angry;
sentences.i: “Friends, surely no one should take offence at a just remark and address the speaker directly with hostile words;
sentences.n: Amphinomus speaks as the peacemaker. οὐκ ἂν δή τις … χαλεπαίνοι is the optative with ἄν used as a mild prohibition: 'no one would (should) be angry'. ἐπὶ ῥηθέντι δικαίῳ is 'at a just word spoken', ῥηθέντι being the aorist passive participle of the verb 'say' (neuter dative, 'what was said'). ἀντιβίοις is 'hostile, confronting', ἐπέεσσι is 'with words', and καθαπτόμενος is 'accosting, assailing' (middle participle). χαλεπαίνοι is the optative of χαλεπαίνω 'be harsh, be angry', from χαλεπός.

sentences.t:
μήτε τι τὸν ξεῖνον στυφελίζετε μήτε τιν’ ἄλλον
δμώων, οἳ κατὰ δώματ’ Ὀδυσσῆος θείοιο.
sentences.l:
Neither in any way the stranger handle roughly, nor any other
of the servants who are throughout the house of divine Odysseus.
sentences.i: Do not handle the stranger roughly, nor any other of the servants in the house of divine Odysseus.
sentences.n: Amphinomus’ plea takes in the whole household, and the stranger is counted among its dependants. μήτε … μήτε with the imperative στυφελίζετε is 'do not … nor …', and μήτε τι is 'in any way at all'. στυφελίζω is 'strike hard, handle roughly'. δμώων is the genitive plural of δμώς 'servant', in τιν’ ἄλλον δμώων 'any other of the servants'. οἳ κατὰ δώματ’ is 'who are throughout the house', δώματα being a plural for one house, and Ὀδυσσῆος θείοιο is 'of divine Odysseus' (θεῖος, genitive in -οιο).

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγετ’, οἰνοχόος μὲν ἐπαρξάσθω δεπάεσσιν,
ὄφρα σπείσαντες κατακείομεν οἴκαδ’ ἰόντες·
sentences.l:
But come, let the wine-pourer pour the first drops into the cups,
so that, having poured libations, we may lie down, going home;
sentences.i: But come, let the cupbearer first pour a few drops into each cup, so that after our libations we may go home to bed;
sentences.n: A practical proposal: end the evening with the libation and go home. ἀλλ’ ἄγετ’ is 'but come', the plural ἄγετε addressing them all. ἐπαρξάσθω is the aorist imperative middle of ἐπάρχομαι 'begin the rite by pouring the first drops', with the dative δεπάεσσιν 'into the cups' (δέπας 'cup', dative plural in -εσσιν). ὄφρα with the subjunctive κατακείομεν (the short-vowel subjunctive of κατάκειμαι) is 'so that we may lie down'; σπείσαντες is the aorist participle of σπένδω, 'having poured libations'.

sentences.t:
τὸν ξεῖνον δὲ ἐῶμεν ἐνὶ μεγάροις Ὀδυσῆος
Τηλεμάχῳ μελέμεν·
sentences.l:
and the stranger let us leave in the halls of Odysseus
to Telemachus to be a care;
sentences.i: and let us leave the stranger in Odysseus’ halls to be Telemachus’ concern;
sentences.n: The stranger is to be left to the master of the house. ἐῶμεν is the subjunctive of ἐάω 'allow, let', used as an exhortation, 'let us leave'; τὸν ξεῖνον is 'the stranger', with the article. Τηλεμάχῳ μελέμεν is 'to be a care to Telemachus', μελέμεν being the epic infinitive of μέλω 'be a care', with the dative of the person who has the care. ἐνὶ μεγάροις Ὀδυσῆος is 'in the halls of Odysseus', a plural for one hall.

sentences.t: τοῦ γὰρ φίλον ἵκετο δῶμα.
sentences.l: for to his dear house he has come.”
sentences.i: for it is to his house that he has come.”
sentences.n: The reason is the logic of hospitality: a host looks after the guest who comes to his house. τοῦ is the genitive of the pronoun, 'of him', Telemachus. φίλον is 'dear', and with a house often means 'one’s own'. ἵκετο is 'came' (aorist of ἵκω), and δῶμα is 'house'. Amphinomus’ speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτο, τοῖσι δὲ πᾶσιν ἑαδότα μῦθον ἔειπε.
sentences.l: So he spoke, and to them all a pleasing speech he uttered.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and what he said pleased them all.
sentences.n: The suitors accept it. ὣς φάτο is 'so he spoke'. τοῖσι … πᾶσιν is 'to them all', ἑαδότα is the perfect participle of ἁνδάνω 'please', so 'a speech that pleased', and ἔειπε is the aorist of εἶπον with the ε doubled for the metre; μῦθον is 'speech'.

sentences.t:
τοῖσιν δὲ κρητῆρα κεράσσατο Μούλιος ἥρως,
κῆρυξ Δουλιχιεύς·
sentences.l:
And for them the mixing-bowl mixed Mulius the hero,
herald of Dulichium;
sentences.i: Then Mulius the hero, a herald of Dulichium, mixed the mixing-bowl for them;
sentences.n: The wine is now mixed by a named servant, introduced with his office and his master: Mulius, a herald, and an attendant of Amphinomus. κρητῆρα is the accusative of κρητήρ, the big mixing-bowl in which wine and water were mixed, and κεράσσατο is the aorist middle of κεράννυμι 'mix', with a doubled σ for the metre. τοῖσιν is 'for them'. ἥρως 'hero' is a title of respect here, given to a man of standing. Δουλιχιεύς is 'man of Dulichium', and κῆρυξ 'herald'.

sentences.t: θεράπων δ’ ἦν Ἀμφινόμοιο·
sentences.l: and an attendant he was of Amphinomus;
sentences.i: and he was Amphinomus’ attendant;
sentences.n: This ties Mulius to the Dulichian Amphinomus. θεράπων is 'attendant', ἦν is 'was', and Ἀμφινόμοιο is the genitive in -οιο.

sentences.t: νώμησεν δ’ ἄρα πᾶσιν ἐπισταδόν·
sentences.l: and he dealt it out then to all, standing by;
sentences.i: and he served all of them, standing beside each man;
sentences.n: νώμησεν is the aorist of νωμάω 'deal out, distribute', ἄρα is 'then', and πᾶσιν is 'to all'. ἐπισταδόν is 'standing by', an adverb from ἐφίστημι: Mulius goes from man to man and stands at each one’s side to serve him.

sentences.t:
οἱ δὲ θεοῖσι
σπείσαντες μακάρεσσι πίον μελιηδέα οἶνον.
sentences.l:
and they, to the gods
having poured libations, the blessed, drank honey-sweet wine.
sentences.i: and they poured a libation to the blessed gods and drank the honey-sweet wine.
sentences.n: οἱ δέ is 'and they'. θεοῖσι … μακάρεσσι is 'to the blessed gods', in the dative plural in -οισι and -εσσι, and σπείσαντες is 'having poured libations'. πίον is the unaugmented aorist of πίνω 'drank'. μελιηδέα οἶνον is 'honey-sweet wine' (μελιηδής, from μέλι 'honey' and ἡδύς 'sweet'). The libation comes before the drinking: the first of the wine goes to the gods.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ σπεῖσάν τ’ ἔπιόν θ’ ὅσον ἤθελε θυμός,
βάν ῥ’ ἴμεναι κείοντες ἑὰ πρὸς δώμαθ’ ἕκαστος.
sentences.l:
But when they had poured libations and drunk, as much as their heart wished,
they set out to go, wishing to lie down, to their own houses, each one.
sentences.i: But when they had poured libations and drunk as much as their hearts wished, they set out for their own houses, each to go to bed.
sentences.n: The evening ends peacefully, each man going to his own house, after a night in which a stool was thrown. σπεῖσάν is the unaugmented aorist of σπένδω and ἔπιον that of πίνω; ὅσον ἤθελε θυμός is 'as much as the heart wished'. βάν is the unaugmented aorist of βαίνω, and ἴμεναι the infinitive of εἶμι 'go', so βάν ῥ’ ἴμεναι is 'they set out to go'. κείοντες is a desiderative participle, 'wishing to lie down' (from κεῖμαι). ἑά is the possessive ὅς, 'their own', agreeing with δώμαθ’ (δώματα, 'houses'), and ἕκαστος 'each one' is singular, spread over the plural subject.
